title: Quiz: ARMv8 Assembly - Fundamentals
prompt: Test your foundational understanding of the ARMv8-A architecture and its basic register file.

questions.question: In the ARMv8-A architecture, which exception level is used for normal user applications with limited privileges?
questions.explanation: EL0 is used for normal user applications and has restricted access to instructions, registers, and memory[cite: 2]. EL1 is for the OS Kernel, EL2 is for a Hypervisor, and EL3 is for the Secure Monitor[cite: 2].
questions.hint: Most programs work at the lowest numbered exception level[cite: 2].

questions.question: Which set of registers are 'callee-saved' and recommended for most of your general work?
questions.explanation: Registers x19-x28 are callee-saved, meaning their values are preserved by any function you call[cite: 2]. Registers x0-x7 are used for arguments and results, and x9-x15 are temporary caller-saved registers[cite: 2].
questions.hint: Look for the block of registers right before the Frame Pointer (x29) and Link Register (x30).

questions.question: What happens if a program attempts to divide an integer by zero using the 'sdiv' or 'udiv' instructions?
options: It generates an exception (a trap) and crashes the program.
It writes a value of 0 to the destination register.
It sets the Z (Zero) condition flag to 1 but leaves the register unchanged.
It writes the maximum possible integer value to the destination register.
questions.explanation: In ARMv8, dividing by 0 does not generate an exception or trap; instead, it simply writes 0 to the destination register[cite: 2].
questions.hint: Unlike many high-level languages, ARMv8 handles this silently without crashing[cite: 2].

questions.question: When debugging with gdb, what is the critical difference between the 'si' (step instruction) and 'ni' (next instruction) commands?
options: 'si' executes the next instruction, while 'ni' proceeds until a function returns if the instruction is a function call.
'si' skips function calls entirely, while 'ni' steps into them.
'si' steps through source code lines, while 'ni' steps through machine code.
'si' executes until the next breakpoint, while 'ni' only executes one instruction.
questions.explanation: Both execute the next instruction, but if that instruction is a function call, 'ni' will proceed until the function returns, whereas 'si' will step directly into the function[cite: 2].
questions.hint: One of these commands will 'step into' a subroutine, while the other will 'step over' it by running the whole subroutine at once[cite: 2].

questions.question: The instruction 'mov x29, sp' is actually an alias provided for readability. What underlying instruction does the assembler translate this to?
questions.explanation: The 'mov' instruction for copying the stack pointer (SP) into x29 is an alias for 'add x29, sp, 0'[cite: 2].
questions.hint: Moving a value is mathematically the same as adding zero to it[cite: 2].
